title: Loss functions
goals: Calculate per-example squared error and mean squared error
Distinguish residual cancellation from a low loss
Separate training loss from independent evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Does knowing a network output tell us whether it is accurate?
prerequisite.answer: No. We also need a target or other evaluation criterion and appropriate examples.

vocabulary: The recorded value a model is intended to predict
Prediction minus target under the sign convention used here
The square of a numerical residual
The average squared error over the evaluated examples

lesson.title: Measure a prediction against a target

blocks.text: A loss assigns a numerical penalty to a prediction compared with a target. For this regression lesson, residual e = prediction - target, and squared error is e squared. Squaring makes both positive and negative residuals contribute nonnegative penalties. We use ordinary mean squared error without a one-half factor.
The mean squared error, or MSE, is (1 + 1 + 4) / 3 = 2. It summarises these three examples, not every possible future input. If targets use cm, residuals use cm and MSE uses square cm.

lesson.title: Do not let signs cancel mistakes

blocks.text: For targets [1, 3] and predictions [2, 2], the mean residual is zero because 1 and -1 cancel. MSE is 1, correctly recording that both predictions miss. A mean residual can describe directional tendency, but it is not a substitute for an error magnitude.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The guard prevents silently ignoring an unmatched example or dividing by zero. It still assumes paired, numeric, valid records. Wrong row alignment produces a meaningless comparison even when list lengths agree.

lesson.title: Compare two candidates on the same cases

blocks.title: Use the same targets and denominator
blocks.caption: Each row evaluates a separate candidate against targets [1, 3, 2]. Q has the lowest MSE on these three cases. The comparison alone does not establish performance on unseen examples.

blocks.label: Candidate R predicts [0, 3, 3] for targets [1, 3, 2]. Calculate residuals, squared errors and MSE. Compare R with the baseline.

lesson.title: Choose a loss for the stated purpose

blocks.text: Squaring gives larger residuals more influence: residual 4 contributes 16, four times the penalty of residual 2. This can be useful when large misses matter, but it can also make outliers influential. Mean absolute error uses absolute residuals instead; it can rank candidates differently.

MSE is appropriate here because targets are numerical quantities. A class identifier such as 0, 1 or 2 may merely name a category; its numeric gap does not automatically measure error severity. Later classification models need a loss suited to their outputs and task.

Training loss measures the cases used to adjust parameters. Validation loss can guide choices, so repeated use makes it development evidence. A reserved final test supports a separate evaluation claim only while it remains outside those choices. Always report the split, number of cases and loss definition.

blocks.label: A model reports MSE zero on its training rows. What has this shown, and why is it insufficient to claim perfect future predictions?

blocks.text: Next week studies local changes in a loss, preparing us to choose a direction for a parameter update.

workbook.title: Calculate a loss
workbook.prompt: For targets [2, 4] and predictions [1, 6], record residuals, squares and MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals are -1 and 2, squares 1 and 4, MSE 2.5.

workbook.title: Expose cancellation
workbook.prompt: Targets [0, 4] have predictions [2, 2]. Compare mean residual and MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals 2 and -2 average to 0; squares 4 and 4 give MSE 4. Both predictions are wrong despite zero mean residual.

workbook.title: Check the denominator
workbook.prompt: A learner totals squared errors 1, 0, 9 and divides by 2 because there are two nonzero errors. Correct the MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: All three evaluated examples count. MSE is 10 / 3, not 5. A zero-error example is still an example.

workbook.title: Compare an unfamiliar evaluation independently
workbook.prompt: Targets are [0, 2, 4]. Model A predicts [1, 2, 3]; model B predicts [0, 2, 2]. Calculate both MSEs and identify the better model under MSE on these cases. Calculate mean absolute errors too. State what changes in the conclusion.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A residuals [1, 0, -1] give MSE 2/3; B [0, 0, -2] gives MSE 4/3, so A is better under MSE. Both mean absolute errors are 2/3, giving a tie under that metric. Neither ranking establishes future performance.

workbook.title: Protect final testing
workbook.prompt: A team tries ten models and picks the one with the lowest final-test MSE. Can that same result be presented as an untouched final evaluation?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. The test informed selection and became development evidence. Preserve the result with that disclosure, freeze the chosen process and use fresh independent evaluation for a new final claim.

teacher.background: Keep paired prediction and target rows visible in both 45-minute sessions. Require residuals, per-row penalties and the denominator before accepting an average. This week uses regression and ordinary MSE; do not introduce a different scaling convention midway.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve why outputs alone do not establish correctness.
Calculate A, B and C row by row. Explain the sign convention and units.
Complete W1 and W2, showing how cancellation hides error.
Run or trace the guarded MSE code; try unequal and empty lists.
Use W3 to recover the full denominator, then compare the visual candidates.
Complete the guided R case and discuss squared versus absolute penalties.
Collect W4 independently, including both metrics and a qualified conclusion.
Use W5 and the exit response. Administer the fresh retry after feedback.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: residuals [-1, 0, 1], squares [1, 0, 1], MSE 2/3, tied with the baseline under MSE. Exit: zero training MSE establishes an exact fit on those recorded targets under the chosen loss; it does not establish performance on unseen cases or correct labels.
misconceptions: Signed residuals can cancel. Apply the specified penalty before averaging.
Ignore perfect predictions in the average
The denominator includes every valid evaluated pair, including zero-error cases.
One metric gives the universal winner
Different losses express different penalties. Choose and disclose the criterion.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires MSEs 2/3 and 4/3, tied MAEs 2/3, and limited claims. Fresh retry: targets [1, 5], predictions [3, 4] give residuals [2, -1], MSE 2.5 and MAE 1.5. Reject averaging the residuals to 0.5 as an error magnitude.
teacher.support: Provide a residual and squared-error table and permit a calculator for fractions. Extension: if both targets and predictions are converted from cm to mm, explain why residuals multiply by 10 and MSE by 100 while candidate ranking stays the same.
